title: Your AI mandate is buying compliance
author: Brian Elliott
summary: Brian Elliott argues that executive mandates to adopt AI secure surface compliance but not the contribution organizations actually need. He opens with BCG's change distance research, which finds executives far more optimistic about change than employees even before details are shared, and Perceptyx data showing that having one's opinions considered matters more than understanding the rationale. He uses Duolingo's reversal of its AI-first performance review policy as a case study and draws on Al Dea's work on leading change to name the contribution gap: since every competitor uses the same models, advantage comes from employees' undocumented knowledge of customers and workflows, which mandates cannot extract. He notes that workers who have watched companies like Cloudflare cut support roles have good reason to hesitate before automating their own expertise. Dea's derailers, especially false growth framing and the say-do gap, compound the credibility problem. Elliott closes with four practices: say what is not changing, visibly reward one contribution, build with AI live in front of the team, and treat resistance as data.
points: BCG found 68 percent of executives feel positive about an upcoming change versus 45 percent of employees, a gap present before anything is announced.
Elliott distinguishes compliance, which mandates can produce, from contribution of tacit workflow knowledge, which they suppress.
He notes Nick Bloom's finding that about two thirds of C-suite executives spend an hour a week or less using AI themselves.
His remedies include a two-column slide showing what stays the same and a leader building with AI live, mistakes included.
Resistance is reframed as a free consulting engagement, since slow adopters often know which problems the rollout ignored.
quotes: 72% of leaders actually think the change program they’re running will work. Only 49% percent of the people on their teams feel the same way.
Explaining the rationale matters less than being heard, which is inconvenient, because explaining is what we’re already doing.

Those executives aren’t idiots and a mandate does move usage. It might even drive up output, especially when you raise the bar on expectations. But fear is not a good long-term motivator and usage isn’t results.

You can get people to comply with using an LLM. It is very hard to get them to contribute their insights about your customers, your workflows, your business. Compliance is surface-level. Commitment creates energy, ownership, and durability.
Asking someone to hand over undocumented expertise is asking them to do something they’ve watched go badly for other people.
The bigger the company, the further executives sit from the work, and the faster “I need to learn this” turns into “they need to do this.
Treat resistance as data. Dea’s reframe: resistance doesn’t have to carry a negative meaning, it can just be information.
